User: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Seattle WA. W-2 from Acme Corp: $82,350. Side income: $11,200 from web design (3 clients). Interest $2,340 (Chase savings), dividends $550 (Interactive Brokers). Home office: 155 sq ft, rent $1,820/month, apartment 680 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,400 (Sallie Mae, 2019–2020); charity $2,000 to Boston Medical Center (donation, have receipt) with receipt; unreimbursed expenses $720. Can you help me fig

ure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
Assistant: Here’s a clear roadmap for your 2024 federal return based on what you shared.

Big picture
- Filing status: Married filing jointly, Seattle WA (no WA state income tax return for wages; your side business may have WA B&O/excise filing—see note at bottom).
- Standard deduction is likely better than itemizing this year.

Deductions and how they apply
- Standard vs itemized
  - 2024 standard deduction (MFJ): $

29,200.
  - What you could itemize with the info given: $2,000 charitable gift. You don’t have mortgage interest or property tax, and WA has no state income tax (you could use the optional state sales tax tables, but even then you’re very unlikely to exceed $29,200). Conclusion: take the standard deduction.

- Above-the-line deductions (these reduce AGI even if you take the standard deduction)
  - Student loan interest: You paid $4,400, but the federal deduction caps at $2,500 for 2024, subject to MAGI phas

eout. Your income appears well below the MFJ phaseout, so you should get the full $2,500.
  - Half of self-employment (SE) tax: Deductible on Schedule 1. Amount depends on your final Schedule C profit (see home office section below). Roughly $389–$440 based on the scenarios below.

- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (separate, taken after the standard deduction)
  - Your web design income should qualify. Expect roughly 20% of your qualified business income (net profit minus half SE tax and certain

other adjustments).
  - Ballpark: about $1,020–$1,160 (see scenarios below). You’ll claim this on Form 8995.

Home office (for your web design business only; not allowed for your W‑2 job)
- Your space: 155 sq ft office in a 680 sq ft apartment = 22.8% business use.
- You rent (no home depreciation), so the key expense is rent:
  - Actual method: 22.8% of annual rent ($1,820 × 12 = $21,840) ≈ $4,978 deduction.
  - Simplified method: $5 × 155 sq ft = $775.
  - The actual method is much larger here, so it’s us

ually the better choice.
- Requirements: regular and exclusive use for business and it’s your principal place of business for the web design work.
- Limitation: the home office deduction can’t create or increase a Schedule C loss; excess indirect expenses carry forward.

Unreimbursed expenses ($720)
- If these are for your web design business (e.g., software, hosting, supplies), deduct them on Schedule C.
- If these are unreimbursed employee (W‑2) job expenses, they are not deductible federally for 2024.

Q

uick numbers to illustrate impact (rounded)
- If $720 are business expenses:
  - Schedule C profit: $11,200 − $4,978 (home office) − $720 = $5,502.
  - SE tax: ≈ $777; half deductible: ≈ $389.
  - QBI deduction: ≈ $1,023.
  - You’ll still take the $29,200 standard deduction.

- If $720 are W‑2-related (not deductible):
  - Schedule C profit: $11,200 − $4,978 = $6,222.
  - SE tax: ≈ $879; half deductible: ≈ $440.
  - QBI deduction: ≈ $1,156.
  - You’ll still take the $29,200 standard deduction.

Which forms

to use
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1: to report Schedule C income and above-the-line deductions (half SE tax, student loan interest)
- Schedule C: web design income and expenses (include the home office deduction on line 30)
- Schedule SE: self-employment tax
- Form 8829: to compute the home office deduction if you use the actual-expense method (not needed if you choose the simplified method)
- Schedule B: required because your interest exceeds $1,500 (report both $2,340 interest and $550 dividends here)
- Form

8995: QBI deduction
- Schedule A: only if you were to itemize (not advantageous here)

A few quick checks
- Dividends: If any portion is qualified, make sure that amount is indicated from your 1099‑DIV (affects tax rate, not the forms list).
- 1099-NEC: If any client issued you one, match your Schedule C gross receipts to those forms (plus any amounts not reported on 1099s).
- WA note: There’s no WA personal income tax, but businesses may have to register/file with the WA Dept. of Revenue and may owe B&O/ex

cise tax even at modest revenue levels. Check current WA DOR thresholds for the “Service and Other Activities” classification.

Open items to confirm
- Is the $720 for your web design business? If yes, I’ll treat it on Schedule C; if not, I’ll exclude it.
- Any other business costs to include (internet portion, software, hosting, equipment, subscriptions, advertising, payment processing fees, insurance)?
- Do you want to use the actual home office method (larger deduction) and file Form 8829, or keep it sim

ple with the $775 simplified method?

If you confirm the $720 category and any extra business expenses, I can firm up the exact deductions and a clean checklist you can use to prepare or review your return.
